Your gut and brain are in constant conversation. Stress can churn your stomach within seconds, and over weeks an unsettled gut can drain your energy and colour your mood. This study explains how the conversation works, what goes wrong, and a practical, evidence-based way to heal it, linked to the tools in this app.

See a doctor first if you have any red flag: blood in your stool or black stools, unexplained weight loss, vomiting that won't stop, difficulty swallowing, anaemia, fever with gut symptoms, symptoms that wake you at night, a new change in bowel habit after 50, or a family history of bowel cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease. If coeliac disease is possible, get tested before cutting out gluten.

Part 1: What the brain–gut axis is

The brain–gut axis (also called the microbiota–gut–brain axis) is the two-way communication network between your brain and your digestive system. It includes nerves, hormones, the immune system and the trillions of microbes living in your gut.

Your gut has its own nervous system, the enteric nervous system: roughly 500 million neurons in the gut wall, more than in the spinal cord. It can run digestion on its own, which is why it is nicknamed the "second brain". But it is constantly talking with the brain in your head.

BRAIN (thoughts, emotions, stress)
↓ nerves · stress hormones ↓   ↑ vagus nerve · immune signals · microbial messengers ↑
GUT (nerves, lining, immune cells, microbes)

Key insight: about 80% of the fibres in the vagus nerve carry messages up from the gut to the brain. Your brain is listening to your gut far more than it is instructing it.

Explore it interactively: The Brain–Gut Axis.

Part 3: What stress does to the gut

When your brain senses threat, it prepares you to fight or run. Digestion is not a priority, so the body puts it on hold or empties the gut fast. That is why fear can bring nausea, "butterflies" or a sudden need for the toilet.

Threat or worry

↓

Fight-or-flight + stress hormones (adrenaline, CRF, cortisol)

↓

Stomach slows, colon may speed up, lining loosens, nerves grow more sensitive

↓

Cramps, bloating, urgency, nausea, appetite changes

↓

The brain notices the symptoms and worries more ↺

Short bursts of this are normal and pass. When stress is constant (conflict at home, overwork, poor sleep, past trauma that keeps the alarm on), the gut can stay in this state, and symptoms become a pattern. See Stress Gut vs. Rest-and-Digest Gut.

Case: Priya, 29, has a churning stomach every Monday morning and loose stools before team meetings. Her tests are normal. Once she starts belly breathing on the commute, eating a small breakfast instead of skipping it, and naming her fear of her manager, the Monday symptoms ease within a few weeks.

Part 4: When the gut talks back

The conversation also runs upward. A gut that is inflamed, sensitised or short of microbial variety sends signals that can affect mood, energy, sleep and stress reactivity.

  • Both directions are real. A 12-year population study found that people with anxiety were more likely to develop new gut disorders, and people with gut disorders were more likely to develop new anxiety and depression.
  • Inflammation and mood. Inflammatory messengers can cause "sickness behaviour": tiredness, withdrawal and low mood. This is one route from gut to brain.
  • Microbes and mood. People with depression tend to have differences in their gut microbes, and in animals, changing microbes changes behaviour. In humans, most of this evidence is still correlational; microbes are one influence among many, not the hidden cause of all low mood.
  • Diet and depression. In the SMILES trial, adults with depression who moved toward a Mediterranean-style diet with dietitian support improved more than those given social support alone.

Gut care can support mental health. It does not replace treatment for depression, anxiety or trauma. If your mood is low most days for two weeks or more, talk to a doctor or counsellor.

Part 5: Disorders of gut–brain interaction

Doctors now use the term disorders of gut–brain interaction (Rome IV) for conditions like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and functional dyspepsia. In these, tests are normal but the gut is over-sensitive and moves irregularly, and the brain processes gut signals as more alarming.

This is not "all in your head". The symptoms are real; they come from the connection between head and gut. That is good news, because it means brain-based treatments work, and they do. Compare the conditions in IBS vs. IBD vs. Coeliac Disease vs. Food Intolerance.

The fear–avoidance loop keeps these conditions going: The Gut–Anxiety Loop. Early adversity, trauma and long-term stress raise the risk, which is why healing the story often helps the gut too.

Part 6: How to heal: six layers

Start with Layer 1 and add one layer at a time. Most people need several layers working together; no single food or supplement fixes the axis.

Layer 1 · Send safety signals

  • Belly Breathing for the Gut: five minutes, twice a day, and before meals.
  • The Rest-and-Digest Meal once a day.
  • Regular sleep and wake times; your gut has a body clock too. See Sleep Wind-Down Routine.

Layer 2 · Feed your microbes

  • 30 Plants a Week: variety matters more than any superfood.
  • Fermented foods on most days if you enjoy them (curd or yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, idli or dosa). In a 10-week Stanford study, a high-fermented-food diet raised microbial diversity and lowered inflammatory markers.
  • Increase fibre slowly over 2–4 weeks and drink water. With IBS, soluble fibre (oats, psyllium, chia) is usually kinder than bran.
  • Cut back on ultra-processed foods, heavy alcohol and late-night eating.

Layer 3 · Move

  • About 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, such as brisk walking. Exercise improves IBS symptoms and microbial diversity.
  • A 10-minute walk after your largest meal helps digestion and blood sugar. See Movement for Mood.

Layer 4 · Retrain the brain side

  • Unhook From Gut Worry whenever a gut sensation sets off fear.
  • Gut-Directed Relaxation daily. For the full benefit, a structured gut-directed hypnotherapy programme (usually 6–12 sessions) has strong evidence for IBS.
  • CBT for IBS, delivered by phone or online, improved symptoms more than usual care in a large UK trial (ACTIB).
  • Gently face what you have been avoiding because of your gut, step by step. See Fear Ladder (Graded Exposure).

Layer 5 · Get the right medical help

  • A low-FODMAP diet with a dietitian: 2–6 weeks of restriction, then reintroduction to find your personal triggers. It is not meant to be lifelong.
  • Peppermint oil capsules can ease IBS pain for some people.
  • Gut–brain medicines: low-dose tricyclic medicines such as amitriptyline improved IBS in the ATLANTIS trial. These act on gut nerves and pain signals, not as "antidepressants for a mental problem".
  • Probiotics: try one product for 4–12 weeks and stop if nothing changes.
  • Take antibiotics when you truly need them, and don't pressure doctors for them when you don't.

Layer 6 · Heal the story and the relationships

  • Chronic stress at home or work keeps the gut on alert. Use Boundary Script and Repair Conversation.
  • If trauma keeps your alarm switched on, work with a trauma-informed therapist; see Trauma Held in the Body.
  • Shame about bowels and bodies keeps people silent and isolated. Tell one safe person, and be honest with your doctor.
  • Eat with others. Shared meals are one of the oldest safety signals we have.

Practical tip: change one thing at a time and give each change about two weeks, so you can tell what actually helps. If symptoms persist after four weeks, take your diary to a doctor or dietitian.

Part 8: Myths and what we know

See Gut Myths vs. What We Know for serotonin, "leaky gut", detoxes, food-sensitivity tests, gluten and probiotics.

Be careful with restriction. Cutting out more and more foods can shrink your microbiome, your nutrition and your life. If you have a history of an eating disorder, avoid elimination diets unless you're working with a specialist team.

Part 9: A relational and faith lens

The body is not the enemy. "I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Ps 139:14). A gut that reacts to threat is a body doing its protective job. Healing means teaching it, gently and repeatedly, that it is safe now.

God cares for the body first. When Elijah collapsed in despair, the angel gave him food and sleep, twice, before any conversation about his calling (1 Kgs 19:5-8). Rest and nourishment are not unspiritual; they are often where healing starts.

The table is a place of safety. Jesus healed and restored people around meals, from Zacchaeus's house to the beach breakfast with Peter (Jn 21:9-17). Eating slowly, with thanks and with others, sends some of the strongest rest-and-digest signals there are.

Rhythm is a gift. Sabbath, regular meals and sleep give the gut and the nervous system the predictable safety they need to repair.
